The Effect of Storage Capacity in Large-Scale Assembly Systems

Isaac Garee

Advised by Andrew Daw and Vishal Gupta · DSO Summer Scholars

1 / 18

Why does storage matter?

Ford F-150 Lightning assembly line. Source: Newsweek

  • Large assembly systems need many distinct components
  • One missing component can delay the entire production line
  • The more components a product requires, the harder it is to have all of them on hand

We examine what happens to the system when you increase the storage of each component

2 / 18

The model

  • One of each kkk components is needed to produce one finished product
  • Component arrivals follow an independent Poisson process
  • Inventory is only stored up to bbb per component
  • Assembly occurs once all components have at least one unit available
3 / 18

Isn't this the coupon collector problem?

  • One cycle can look like a coupon collector
  • We wait for every missing component type to arrive
  • Repeated arrivals do not finish the cycle while one type is still missing

Once every type has appeared, the problem ends; duplicates do not affect another round.

4 / 18

What do the buffers change?

  • Building a truck consumes only one unit of each component
  • Extra components remain in storage and carry over into the next cycle
  • The rollover couples consecutive cycles

One unit of each type is consumed, while extra units remain and affect the next cycle.

Storage gives the system memory, making it harder than a classic coupon collector.

In short

Storage sets the scale

  • Storage capacity b controls the typical number of missing components
  • The typical number grows on the scale k1/b
  • More storage means fewer missing components
